title: Responding to threats
blurb: Choose and justify avoid, reduce, transfer or accept for any threat, and tell proactive responses from a reactive fallback plan.
question: A council is building a riverside footbridge. It moves the riverbank works out of the flood season, adds extra weld inspections, signs a fixed-price contract for the steelwork and simply notes a possible two-day delay to signage, with a plan to use temporary signs if it happens. Which response is each of these, and which is reactive?

teach.h: Respond in proportion, before or after
teach.body: Once a threat is analysed, its risk owner chooses a response whose cost and effort are proportionate to the exposure and fit the organisation's risk appetite. Responses are PROACTIVE (planned and taken now, before the risk occurs, to change its probability or impact) or REACTIVE (planned now but used only if the risk occurs, such as a fallback plan, usually paid for from contingency). The four threat responses are avoid, reduce, transfer and accept.

teach.h: The four responses to a threat

children.label: Avoid
children.sub: change the plan so it can't happen or can't hurt

children.label: Transfer
children.sub: pass the financial impact to a third party

children.label: Accept
children.sub: a deliberate choice to take no proactive action

teach.caption: Reduce is often called mitigate. Accepted threats are still recorded, owned and watched.

teach.body: AVOID: change the scope, method or schedule so the threat disappears, such as using proven technology instead of an untested product. REDUCE: act now to make it less likely or less damaging, such as surveys, testing, training or prototypes. TRANSFER: pay a third party better placed to carry the financial impact, through insurance, a fixed-price contract or a warranty. ACCEPT: decide to tolerate it because nothing worthwhile can be done or the response would cost more than the exposure.

rows.label: Cost
values: Spent whether or not it occurs

teach.caption: A trigger (an agreed warning sign) tells the risk owner when to switch to the fallback plan.

rows.label: Riverbank works moved out of flood season
Two-day signage delay noted and watched
Temporary signs used if the delay happens

teach.note: Ask: does it remove the threat, shrink it, hand its cost to someone else, or tolerate it? And is it done now, or only if the risk occurs?

teach.h: A rule of thumb, not a rule
teach.caption: Unlikely but severe threats (a fire, a flood) are classic candidates for insurance. Always weigh the response's cost against the exposure.

steps.label: Accept
steps.sub: Signage may arrive two days late

steps.label: Plan fallback
steps.sub: Temporary signs agreed with the council

steps.label: If triggered
steps.sub: Use the fallback; draw on contingency

teach.h: Residual risk, secondary risk and life cycles
teach.body: Most responses leave some RESIDUAL risk, which stays on the register with its owner. A response can also create a SECONDARY risk: insurance brings an excess and conditions; a new supplier brings a new dependency. In a linear project, responses are planned in definition, costed into the baseline and reviewed at gates. In an iterative project, teams reduce threats by tackling the riskiest backlog items first or building a quick prototype, and avoid them by deferring a risky feature.

teach.text: Classic confusions: TRANSFER doesn't make the threat vanish; it moves the financial impact (at a price) and reputational damage usually stays with you. REDUCE and mitigate mean the same thing. ACCEPT is a deliberate, recorded decision, not neglect. And a FALLBACK plan is reactive: it is prepared now but only used if the risk occurs.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Name the response and define it (e.g. transfer: pass the financial impact to a third party).
Apply it to the scenario with a concrete action (insurance, fixed-price contract).
Say whether it is proactive (now) or reactive (only if the risk occurs).
Justify it: proportionate cost versus exposure, within risk appetite.
Mention the residual or secondary risk and the owner who monitors it.
Threat responses: avoid, reduce (mitigate), transfer, accept.
Proactive: taken now to change probability or impact. Reactive: a fallback used only if the risk occurs.
Transfer moves the financial impact at a cost; it doesn't remove the threat.
Accept is a deliberate decision, often backed by a fallback plan and contingency.
Residual risk remains after a response; secondary risk is created by it.

summary: You can now match any threat to avoid, reduce, transfer or accept and justify the choice on cost and exposure. You can also separate proactive responses from a reactive fallback plan, and spot residual and secondary risks.

A.q: A school extension's groundworks could be flooded if done in winter. The team reschedules them to the summer holidays. Which response is this?
options: Reduce
Avoid
Transfer
Accept
A.why: Changing the schedule so the flooding threat can no longer affect the groundworks is avoidance.

whyNot.0: Reduce lowers probability or impact but leaves the threat in place; here it is removed.
whyNot.2: Nothing is passed to a third party.
whyNot.3: Accepting would mean doing the works in winter and tolerating the threat.

A.q: Complete the statement: a response that passes the financial impact of a threat to a third party, usually for a fee, is called…
options: avoid
reduce
accept
transfer
A.why: Transfer passes the financial consequences (and sometimes management) of a threat to a third party, such as an insurer or a fixed-price contractor.

whyNot.0: Avoid removes the threat by changing the plan; no third party carries it.
whyNot.1: Reduce lowers probability or impact through the project's own actions.
whyNot.2: Accept means the project carries the threat itself.

options: Actions prepared now, used only if the risk occurs
A reserve of money held in the project budget
Actions taken now to lower a risk's probability
A contract clause passing the risk on to a supplier
A.why: A fallback plan is a reactive response: it is agreed in advance but only put into action if the risk occurs.

whyNot.1: A reserve of money is contingency, which often pays for the fallback but is not the plan itself.
whyNot.2: Acting now to lower probability is a proactive reduce response.
whyNot.3: Passing the risk to a supplier through a contract is transfer.

B.q: A software team writes automated tests and pairs junior developers with seniors to cut the chance of defects in a payments module. Which response is this?
options: Transfer
Accept
Reduce
Avoid
B.why: Testing and pairing lower the probability (and impact) of defects without removing the threat entirely: that is reduction.

whyNot.0: No third party takes on the financial impact.
whyNot.1: The team is acting proactively, so it is not simply accepting the threat.
whyNot.3: The payments module is still being built, so the threat still exists; it is reduced, not avoided.

B.q: A PM takes no proactive action on a low-probability, low-impact threat, but records it, names an owner and reviews it monthly. Which statement is correct?
options: This is avoidance, because no money is spent
This is poor practice: every threat must be reduced
This is transfer, because the register now holds it
This is acceptance, a valid deliberate response
B.why: Accept is a legitimate, deliberate choice when a response would cost more than the exposure. The threat is still owned and monitored.

whyNot.0: Avoidance changes the plan to remove the threat; here the threat remains.
whyNot.1: Responses must be proportionate; spending to reduce a trivial threat may waste money.
whyNot.2: Recording a risk doesn't transfer it; transfer needs a third party to carry the impact.

B.q: Which of these is a REACTIVE response to a threat?
options: Buying insurance before construction starts
Switching to a proven supplier at the outset
Starting a standby generator when power fails
Running extra training before the system launch
B.why: Starting the standby generator is only done once the power failure (the risk) has occurred, so it is a reactive fallback.

whyNot.0: Insurance is arranged in advance: a proactive transfer.
whyNot.1: Changing supplier at the outset is a proactive avoid response.
whyNot.3: Training in advance is a proactive reduce response.

C.q: A theatre is converting a listed building and signs a fixed-price contract with the builder for the main works. What is the best explanation of the effect on the threat of cost overruns?
options: The overrun threat is avoided altogether
The builder bears overrun costs, at a premium
The probability of any overrun is cut to zero
The theatre accepts all overrun costs itself
C.why: A fixed price transfers the financial impact of most overruns to the builder, who prices that risk into the contract. The threat still exists.

whyNot.0: Overruns can still happen; only who pays for them changes.
whyNot.2: The contract doesn't make overruns less likely; it changes who bears their cost.
whyNot.3: The theatre has deliberately moved the cost of overruns to the builder, so it is not accepting them.

C.q: An outdoor product launch faces bad-weather threats. Which TWO of these are PROACTIVE responses? 1 Moving the event indoors in advance. 2 A plan to hire a marquee if it rains on the day. 3 Insuring the event against cancellation. 4 Drawing on contingency after a storm.
options: 2 and 4
1 and 2
1 and 3
3 and 4
C.why: Moving indoors (avoid) and buying insurance (transfer) are both done in advance, before the risk occurs, so they are proactive.

whyNot.0: Both the marquee plan and drawing contingency are only used once the weather turns: they are reactive.
whyNot.1: Moving indoors is proactive, but the marquee plan is a reactive fallback.
whyNot.3: Insurance is proactive, but drawing on contingency after the storm is reactive.

C.q: A rail project insures its tunnel boring machine against breakdown. The insurer insists that only one approved contractor, who is often fully booked, may service it. What is this availability problem?
options: A residual risk left after the response
A secondary risk created by the response
An issue that must be escalated at once
An opportunity to share with the insurer
C.why: The insurance (a transfer response) has created a new threat that did not exist before: a secondary risk, which needs its own owner and response.

whyNot.0: Residual risk is what is left of the ORIGINAL risk after the response, not a new risk the response creates.
whyNot.2: Nothing has gone wrong yet; it is an uncertain future problem, so it is a risk, not an issue.
whyNot.3: A limited choice of contractor is a threat to the schedule, not a positive opportunity.

reteach.title: Think of a family road trip
reteach.question: A family is driving 400 miles to a holiday cottage in an old car that might break down. What are their four options, and what is their plan B?

blocks.h: Four ways to handle a breakdown threat
blocks.body: They could AVOID it by taking the train instead. They could REDUCE it by getting the car serviced and the tyres checked before setting off. They could TRANSFER it by joining a breakdown recovery service, so someone else bears the cost of a tow. Or they could ACCEPT it and just go. Whatever they choose, a sensible family also has a FALLBACK: the nearest garage noted and £200 kept aside (contingency) in case the car stops.

blocks.text: Joining the recovery service doesn't stop the car breaking down: it moves the cost of the tow. That is why transfer is never the same as avoid.

explain.body: Change the plan (scope, method, location, schedule or supplier) so the threat can't happen or can't affect the objectives. It is the most complete response, but it may cost money or give up some scope or benefit.

steps.label: Threat
steps.sub: Untested platform may fail at launch

test.q: Which action AVOIDS the threat that an untested software platform fails at launch?
options: Testing the new platform more thoroughly
Using the organisation's proven platform
Insuring against losses if the platform fails
Preparing a manual workaround if it fails
test.why: Switching to the proven platform removes the threat of the untested one failing: that is avoidance.

whyNot.0: More testing lowers the probability but keeps the threat: that is reduce.
whyNot.2: Insurance moves the financial impact to an insurer: that is transfer.
whyNot.3: A workaround used only if the platform fails is a reactive fallback plan.

explain.body: Take action now to lower the probability, the impact, or both. Examples: surveys, prototypes, testing, training, extra inspections, spare stock. The threat remains, but smaller; what is left is the residual risk.

steps.label: Before
steps.sub: Unknown ground: high probability of costly surprises

steps.label: Residual
steps.sub: Lower probability, still owned and watched

test.q: Before designing a building's foundations, the team commissions a ground survey to lower the chance of nasty surprises. Which response is this?
options: Avoid
Accept
Transfer
Reduce
test.why: The survey lowers the probability (and likely impact) of unexpected ground conditions without removing the threat: that is reduction.

whyNot.0: The building still needs foundations in that ground, so the threat hasn't been removed.
whyNot.1: Commissioning a survey is proactive action, not acceptance.
whyNot.2: No third party takes on the financial impact.

explain.body: Pass the financial impact (and sometimes the management) of a threat to a third party better able to carry it: insurance, fixed-price contracts, warranties, bonds. It costs a premium or a higher price, and some impact, such as reputational damage, usually stays with the project.

explain.h: What transfer does and doesn't do

test.q: Which statement about TRANSFER is TRUE?
options: It usually costs money, such as a premium or fee
It removes the threat from the project entirely
It is free, because a third party takes it on
It moves all reputational damage to the supplier
test.why: The third party charges for carrying the risk, through a premium, a fee or a higher contract price.

whyNot.1: The threat can still occur; only who bears the financial impact changes.
whyNot.2: Third parties price the risk in, so transfer is rarely free.
whyNot.3: Reputational damage usually stays with the organisation whose project it is.

explain.body: Accept when a response would cost more than the exposure, or nothing worthwhile can be done. It is still recorded, owned and monitored. A reactive fallback plan, funded from contingency and launched by a trigger, can sit behind an accepted threat.

items.label: likely cost if the threat occurs
response costs more than the exposure

explain.caption: Illustrative numbers only: the point is proportionality, not the arithmetic.

test.q: Why might a project choose to accept a threat rather than reduce it?
options: Accepted threats no longer need to be monitored
Acceptance moves the threat on to the sponsor
Accepting a threat stops it from ever occurring
Reducing it would cost more than the exposure
test.why: Responses must be proportionate. If reducing a threat costs more than the damage it could do, accepting it (often with a fallback) is sensible.

whyNot.0: Accepted threats are still owned and monitored in case they grow.
whyNot.1: Acceptance doesn't change ownership; the risk owner still manages it.
whyNot.2: Accepting a threat does nothing to its probability.
